title: Real-Time Impersonation Detection and Automated Alerting in IoTEnabled Polling Systems
abstract: This paper presents the design and implementation of an IoT-based fraud resistance e-voting system integrated with biometric and RFID authentication to ensure the integrity of the democratic process. Traditional voting systems are often vulnerable to identity theft, proxy voting, and manual tallying errors. The proposed system addresses these challenges by employing a multi-factor authentication protocol: an RFID layer for voter identification and a fingerprint biometric layer for person-to-document verification. Utilizing an ESP32 microcontroller, the system captures voter data and compares it against a pre-enrolled database. A unique feature of this system is its real-time fraud detection mechanism; if a user attempts to cast a secondary vote, the system triggers a buzzer alarm, sends a notification via GSM to authorities, and logs the incident to a remote cloud server via Wi-Fi. Experimental results demonstrate that the system successfully prevents duplicate voting and provides a transparent, automated platform for real-time result monitoring, significantly reducing the potential for electoral malpractice.

title: langscript v1.0: Complete Whitepaper & Proposal — A Cognitive Protocol for the Age of Human-Agent Collaboration
abstract: langscript is a semi-structured, declarative interaction language designed to occupy the space between natural language and executable code — a space called "The Middle Way." It is not a programming language and it is not prose. It is a cognitive protocol: a set of human-readable, machine-interpretable conventions that give Large Language Models the structural signals they need to reason reliably, while preserving the expressive fluidity that makes human thought worth capturing. langscript draws on principles from Object-Oriented Programming — encapsulation, inheritance, dot-notation — and reframes them as Object-Oriented Prompting (OOPrompting), a paradigm in which the user constructs semantic objects that an LLM can parse as executable logic rather than casual chatter. The result is a dramatic improvement in intent clarity, contextual continuity, tone alignment, and cross-model portability. This whitepaper presents the complete v1.0 foundational specification of langscript, synthesized from earlier draft formulations. It covers the problem space, core constructs (session, context, subtask, pipeline, task, meta), design philosophy, and practical applications for human-agent collaboration.

title: Opportunities and Perspectives
abstract: The convergence of technological, financial, and interdisciplinary efforts, combined with the rapid evolution of algorithms and hardware, strongly suggests that the achievement of TAI could not be a question of “if”, but rather of “when” and “how”. Concerning “when”, the authors in ( Gruetzemacher et al., 2019 ) estimated AI capabilities over the next decade (2019–2029) and made questions for forecasting five scenarios of TAI. The same author proposed and outlined in ( Gruetzemacher, 2019 ) a novel framework for forecasting TAI, which integrates a variety of forecasting techniques into a cohesive and holistic approach, aiming to enhance the reliability and comprehensiveness of predictions in this rapidly evolving domain. The famous prediction engine Metaculus 1 also provides forecasts of AI-based technologies and their impacts on our civilization.

title: The Construction and Application of the Smart Classroom Reasoning Graph Based on Deep Learning
abstract: This paper designs a behavior pattern recognition algorithm that combines K-Means and lag sequence analysis. The K-Means algorithm is utilized to conduct unsupervised clustering on temporal behavior sequences with similar behavioral characteristics to discover potential behavior categories and pattern types. Subsequently, the lag sequence analysis method was used to model the temporal relationship of the clustering results, explore the transition probability and sequence dependence between behaviors, and thereby identify the behavior transition patterns with statistical significance. Finally, in order to verify the effectiveness of the algorithm, a visual analysis of real classroom videos was conducted.

title: Transformer-based Photovoltaic Power Forecasting Model through Explicit Period Modeling
abstract: Accurate photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting is essential for ensuring the safe and stable operation of power systems. However, PV power generation exhibits complex temporal dynamics, which makes precise forecasting a challenging task. To address this, this paper proposes a Transformer-based forecasting model that incorporates explicit period modeling. First, a temporal querying technique is used to extract the periodic shift component corresponding to the input sequence from a learnable periodic shift vector. Next, both the extracted periodic shift component and the input sequence are divided into patches and embedded separately. In the temporal attention mechanism, the embedded periodic shift patches serve as queries, while the embedded input sequence patches act as keys and values. This design enables the model to capture both global stable periodic patterns and robust local temporal dynamics for each PV site. Finally, the learned multi-scale temporal features are passed through a projection module to generate the forecasted power values. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves state-of-the-art forecasting performance with moderate computational and memory overhead, outperforming existing advanced models based on multilayer perceptions and Transformers.

title: Separate-Align Embedding Based Backdoor Attacks in Large Language Model-based Agents
abstract: Although Large Language Model-based agents have demonstrated outstanding performance in reasoning, tool usage, and task planning, they are still vulnerable to being easily poisoned by backdoor attackers. Existing backdoor attack methods either directly alter the model’s final output (i.e., Outputguided Attack) or manipulate the model’s internal decisionmaking process (i.e., Thought-guided Attack). Output-guided attacks rely on significant query triggers, causing contaminated and clean samples to become entangled in the embedding space, leading to unstable backdoor activation and false triggers. To address these issues, we propose Separate-Align Embedding (SAE) based backdoor attacks in LLM-based agents. Particularly, SAE introduces an embedding-level separation constraint to disentangle poisoned from clean samples, which is significant to improve clean accuracy and reduce the poisoned data rate. Additionally, we incorporate an alignment constraint to align poisoned embeddings with target response embeddings, thereby enhancing the attack success rate (ASR) and trigger activation rate (TAR). We evaluate SAE across three different agent tasks and multiple LLM-based agents. Experimental results show that our SAE, on average, improves the clean accuracy rate by 3%, ASR by $\mathbf{1 2 \%}$, and TAR by $\mathbf{1 8 \%}$ compared to the best baseline with only 1% poisoned data.

title: A Literature Review about Federated Learning in Recommendation Systems
abstract: The increasing demand for personalized services has led to widespread adoption of recommendation systems across various domains, from entertainment to e-commerce. Traditional centralized implementations, however, raise privacy and data management concerns. This study investigates federated learning as a decentralized approach for recommendation systems, where multiple clients collaboratively train a global model while keeping their local data private. We provide a detailed analysis of different federated learning partitions-horizontal, vertical, and transfer learning-and examine techniques for integrating local updates into a global model. The paper also explores challenges such as heterogeneity, communication overhead, and privacy-preserving mechanisms, highlighting their impact on model performance and deployment. By synthesizing current approaches and evaluating their applicability in the context of ecommerce recommendation systems, this work offers actionable insights for designing scalable, privacy-aware, and adaptive federated learning frameworks, contributing to both practical implementation and academic research in the field.

title: Putnam 2025 Problems in Rocq using Opus 4.6 and Rocq-MCP
abstract: We report on an experiment in which Claude Opus~4.6, equipped with a suite of Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools for the Rocq proof assistant, autonomously proved 10 of 12 problems from the 2025 Putnam Mathematical Competition. The MCP tools, designed with Claude by analyzing logs from a prior experiment on miniF2F-Rocq, encode a "compile-first, interactive-fallback" strategy. Running on an isolated VM with no internet access, the agent deployed 141 subagents over 17.7 hours of active compute (51.6h wall-clock), consuming approximately 1.9 billion tokens. All proofs are publicly available.

title: MACHINE LEARNING-BASED FRAUD DETECTION SYSTEM FOR SECURE BANKING TRANSACTIONS
abstract: This research investigates the potential of machine learning to identify misconduct in banking data, thereby enhancing the reliability and security of financial transactions. The enormous volumes of transaction data that financial institutions receive have made it increasingly challenging for them to detect fraudulent activity due to the exponential expansion of online payment systems and digital banking. Machine learning techniques frequently surpass conventional rule-based systems when it pertains to intricate and perpetually evolving fraud patterns. In this study, a variety of machine learning techniques are implemented to analyze transaction data and detect anomalous patterns. Random forests, decision trees, and neural networks are all examples of such systems. By employing feature selection, data preprocessing, and model training, the proposed method improves identification accuracy and reduces false positive rates. Machine learning algorithms have the potential to identify suspicious financial transactions by revealing patterns and anomalies that were previously unknown, as indicated by experiments. If these concepts are executed, banking will be more secure, clients will have greater confidence in their institutions, and expenses will decrease.

title: The Quantum-Resistant Storefront: Transitioning E-Commerce Security Frameworks for the Post-Quantum Era
abstract: The advent of quantum computing presents a formidable threat to the security of digital information, particularly for the e-commerce sector, which relies heavily on cryptographic protocols for secure transactions and data protection. This systematic literature review examines the transition from current cryptographic standards to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) within e-commerce security frameworks. The study addresses the urgent need for quantum-resistant algorithms to safeguard against the looming "Q-Day," when quantum computers will be capable of breaking widely used public-key encryption schemes. Through a systematic review of peer-reviewed literature, this paper synthesizes existing research on the vulnerabilities of current e-commerce security, the development and standardization of PQC algorithms, and the strategic roadmaps for their implementation. Our findings reveal a consensus on the theoretical robustness of PQC candidates, such as lattice-based, code-based, and hash-based cryptography. However, significant challenges remain in the practical integration of these algorithms into legacy e-commerce systems, including performance overhead and the need for crypto-agility. The review highlights the critical role of standardization bodies like NIST in guiding the transition and the necessity for proactive, phased adoption by online businesses. This paper concludes by discussing the implications for the e-commerce industry and outlining a research agenda focused on developing and implementing practical, efficient, and secure quantum-resistant security frameworks for the post-quantum era.

title: AI-Native Visual Feedback Loop (AIVFL) — The AI Sees What It Builds
abstract: AIVFL donne la vue aux IA. AIVFL-WAN leur donne la portee. Local, global, meme boucle. AI-Native Visual Feedback Loop (AIVFL) We introduce AIVFL, a missing primitive enabling AI agents to directly observe the real-time visual output of the systems they control — mobile apps, web UIs, dashboards, training curves — and iterate autonomously against a specification. Unlike traditional coding assistants, AIVFL establishes a closed-loop visual feedback cycle, allowing the agent to see what it produces and correct itself continuously. Key properties: - Portable: works across LAN, WAN, subnets, WiFi ADB, VPN tunnels, any topology - Transport-agnostic: scrcpy, RTSP, Miracast, WebRTC, Tailscale, any screen-capture method - Distance-agnostic: USB-local > same LAN > cross-subnet > remote WAN > intercontinental - Sovereign: fully local, zero cloud dependency, zero data exfiltration - Invisible: supports offscreen capture (window in background) - Stable: single instance, PID-managed, clean start/stop No existing AI coding assistant implements this closed-loop visual feedback mechanism. Prior art analysis included. All rights reserved. AIVFL-WAN Extension We extend AIVFL beyond local execution to full WAN-scale debugging. The loop remains stable across heterogeneous network environments, including LAN, WAN, VPN tunnels, CGNAT, IPv6, and intercontinental links. Transport remains agnostic (scrcpy, RTSP, WebRTC, Tailscale), and the system preserves full sovereignty with zero cloud dependency. This establishes AIVFL as a distance-agnostic primitive for autonomous visual iteration, capable of operating across arbitrary physical and network boundaries without altering the underlying mechanism. CLAIMS: 📄 OEIL + FORGE — 14 Claims (Version Zenodo) Version structurée, neutre, opposable, prête pour archivage scientifique. Claim 1 — AI Visual Feedback Loop (AIVFL) A validation tool invoked by a vision model to assess, stabilize, and certify visual interpretations without altering the model’s identity or autonomy. Claim 2 — Evidence Anchoring Principle All evaluations are grounded in a single immutable piece of evidence (image, text, or data), which acts as the unique source of truth for the entire reasoning process. Claim 3 — Mode‑Dependent Evaluation The system’s output depends on the operational mode selected (e.g., certification, analysis), while the underlying evidence remains unchanged. Claim 4 — Chérie (VISION+) A dedicated vision model acting as the primary perceptual entity, independent from validation tools and external evaluators. Claim 5 — OEIL (Operational Evaluation and Image Logic) A certified evaluation mode where Chérie invokes AIVFL to produce deterministic, validated visual assessments. Claim 6 — Six‑Law Codex A rule set ensuring coherence, non‑drift, non‑agentivity, reproducibility, and structural stability across all evaluations. Claim 7 — FORGE (Autonomous Specialist Generation) A pipeline enabling the creation of modular AI specialists through structured datasets, local training, and controlled behavioral shaping. Claim 8 — Thinkbox Generalization Primitive A mechanism enabling layered reasoning without state drift, allowing models to explore multiple interpretative layers while remaining anchored to the initial evidence. Claim 9 — Temporal Coherence Protocol A protocol ensuring consistency of evaluations across time, preventing contradictions between sequential outputs. Claim 10 — Multi‑Agent Parallel Evaluation Multiple agents can evaluate the same evidence simultaneously, each operating in its own mode, producing complementary outputs. Claim 11 — Sovereign GGUF Deployment Local, offline, reproducible deployment of models in GGUF format, ensuring independence from cloud infrastructures. Claim 12 — LACF (Local Autonomous Cognitive Framework) A framework for local dataset enrichment, training, validation, and export, ensuring full sovereignty over the cognitive pipeline. Claim 13 — OEIL Composition Primitive OEIL is defined as the operational composition of Chérie (vision) and AIVFL (validation tool). The composition is modular, reversible, and architecture‑agnostic. Claim 14 — Dual‑Mode Evidence Evaluation A single piece of evidence can generate distinct certified outputs depending on the operational mode (e.g., defensive validation vs. critical analysis). The evidence remains constant; the mode determines the behavior. Multiple agents may evaluate the same evidence in parallel, producing coherent, non‑contradictory perspectives.

title: ALBERT-TextCNN Based Grassroots Governance Topic Identification and Cultural Factor Analysis System for Social Media
abstract: Grassroots social governance in China increasingly relies on culturally-informed approaches that integrate traditional values with modern administrative practices. However, the manual analysis of governance documents to identify topics and embedded cultural factors is labor-intensive and lacks consistency. This paper presents a novel hybrid deep learning framework that combines ALBERT (A Lite BERT) with TextCNN for automated topic classification and cultural factor recognition in Chinese social governance texts. Our approach addresses the dual challenge of capturing both global semantic context and local linguistic patterns through a three-component architecture: (1) ALBERT-based contextual encoding for deep semantic understanding, (2) multi-scale TextCNN for extracting discriminative n-gram features, and (3) a cultural-sensitive word attention module constructed from a domain-specific lexicon of 468 culturally-loaded terms. We construct and annotate a comprehensive dataset of 2,847 governance documents spanning five major topics (Community Construction, Public Services, Conflict Mediation, Cultural Activities, and Policy Implementation) and nine cultural factors (Clan Concept, Rural Elite Culture, Folk Customs, Etiquette Norms, Collective Spirit, Patriotic Sentiment, Harmony Concept, Moral Governance, and Traditional Festivals). Experimental results demonstrate that our hybrid model achieves 81.7% accuracy in topic classification and 0.843 macro-averaged F1-score in cultural factor recognition, significantly outperforming baseline methods including BERT, RoBERTa, and standalone TextCNN by margins of 3.2% and 4.6% respectively. Ablation studies reveal that the cultural-sensitive module contributes 8.2% performance gain, while the multi-scale convolutional component improves results by 2.4% over transformer-only architectures. Confusion matrix analysis indicates that recognition challenges primarily arise from semantically overlapping categories such as Moral Governance and Harmony Concept, reflecting genuine philosophical interconnections rather than model deficiencies. Our work contributes both methodologically—by demonstrating the effectiveness of hybrid architectures for domain-specific text analysis—and practically, by providing an automated tool for enhancing cultural sensitivity in governance practices. The system enables officials to assess policy communications for cultural appropriateness, retrieve relevant governance precedents, and facilitate knowledge transfer across diverse regional contexts. This research establishes a foundation for AI-assisted cultural analysis in public administration and opens avenues for cross-disciplinary collaboration between natural language processing and social sciences.

title: Navigating Standards in Engineering Design Through Latent Textual Topology and Large Language Models
abstract: Abstract In engineering design, standards are instrumental in providing technical definitions and guidelines to designers, manufacturers, and users, reflecting best practices that are widely recognized. These standards, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, encapsulate the current state of technological expertise and aim to promote safety, reliability, productivity, and efficiency in both component and system design. Despite the clear value of standards, the vast quantity and diversity of these documents present significant challenges for designers in retrieving and implementing the appropriate standards for their projects. Moreover, the significant amount of time design engineers exhaust navigating through technical documentation highlights the necessity for more effective methods of engaging with the textual knowledge base represented by engineering standards, as the current manual process is inefficient and time-intensive. This presents an even greater challenge for small- and medium-sized enterprises lacking the requisite personnel to adeptly navigate evolving standards. To bridge this gap, this research develops a fundamental understanding of language embeddings and large language models (LLMs) to assist in navigating engineering standards. This work examines the efficacy of utilizing LLMs, such as bidirectional encoder representations from transformers, to navigate the extensive corpus of standards and requirements. It also examines three semantic-based approaches for engineering standard retrieval and further validates these approaches through an industry case study. Additionally, the standards augmented requirements generator tool is presented, which provides a domain-specific approach to leveraging retrieval-augmented generation in design contexts.

title: Modifying Simple Preference Optimization with Adaptive Margins
abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences remains an essential step for their practical deployment. Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has established itself as a widely adopted alignment methodology. Simple Preference Optimization (SimPO) further diminishes training expenses while enhancing alignment efficacy. However, SimPO’s performance is highly sensitive to data quality, and its predefined trade-off parameter of margin lacks adaptive adjustment across data of varying quality. In this paper, we propose an adaptive method wherein the target margin is dynamically modulated during training based on data quality. This approach enables the model to more effectively assimilate preference knowledge from highquality data while mitigating the detrimental impact of lowquality data on the model’s generative capabilities. Our method is built upon the SimPO framework, achieving performance improvements with minimal additional code, requiring no external knowledge, and incurring no additional training costs.

title: A Fault Propagation Path Identification Method for A320 Air Conditioning System Based on Partial Rank Correlation Hybrid Search Algorithm
abstract: The aircraft air conditioning system is highly complex, and traditional causal structure learning algorithms struggle to handle multivariable interference and high data heterogeneity in nonlinear systems. These challenges often lead to deviations in causal network construction and reduced modeling accuracy. To address this, a hybrid search algorithm based on partial rank correlation coefficients is proposed for causal modeling of the air conditioning system. By integrating the system's physical structure with causal network principles, three fundamental causal patterns—transmission, multi-input, and multi-output structures—are identified to guide network construction. Conditional independence tests using partial rank correlation coefficients, combined with the d-separation principle, are employed to build the causal skeleton. A greedy search algorithm refines edge directions, completing the network structure. An elite ant colony optimization strategy is further introduced to enhance fault path inference. Experiments using QAR data from the A320 air conditioning system show that the proposed method significantly reduces causal misjudgments and improves the accuracy of both network learning and fault propagation inference, providing theoretical support for intelligent fault diagnosis and maintenance.

title: Federated Split Learning: Distributed Local Training for Low Computational Unit Clients
abstract: Federated Learning (FL) and Split Learning (SL) are two of the most novel methods of the distributed Learning paradigm. FL and SL both works with multi-participant network settings while also ensuring user data privacy. The FL thrives when a large number of clients participate in the learning process. However, as different clients can have different computational capacities, they can fail to complete the training due to hardware limitations, affecting the overall distributed learning process. SL is useful in this case, as its working method is to distribute workloads between different parties. This work dives deeper into the architecture level of these two paradigms and combines them both to build a new framework. The new framework, called Federated Split Learning (FSL), is a novel and robust way to integrate SL’s workload offloading mechanism in FL’s local training. This will allow for low computing devices in FL to partake in complex tasks despite hardware limitations, allowing more client participation in FL. This work presents the proposed hybrid framework that improves FL by implementing SL for its low load clients, the implementation of the framework, and proofs to guarantee that it is fully functional and efficient.

title: Building an analogue simulator of a photonic quantum computer with transparent tape, maple syrup, and cat lasers, and implementing first quantum algorithms in the classroom
abstract: This work presents the implementation of single-qubit gates, including $R_x$ and $R_z$ gates realized using transparent adhesive tape, and $R_y$ gates obtained with optically active maple and agave solutions. These gates form the native gate set of a simple photonic system and are subsequently used to construct a Hadamard gate. Two forms of two-qubit gates are introduced using a combination of a calcite crystal and transparent tape. The setups employ both the polarization and the path degree of freedom of a photon as qubits, illustrating how readily accessible materials can be used to manipulate and transform the quantum information they convey. Calculations are performed to determine the birefringence of two different types of tape and to quantify the specific rotations introduced by multiple layers of transparent tape. Finally, simple algorithms and exercises are proposed for students. These experimental setups are designed to facilitate hands-on manipulation of quantum effects while lowering the barrier to accessing quantum systems, with total costs kept below \$50 CAD for the single-qubit gates and below \$100 CAD for all experiments combined. The configurations presented serve as an analog simulator of a photonic quantum computer: although the laser beams used can be described classically, all theoretical considerations and experimental procedures remain valid for quantized systems employing single-photon emitters and single-photon detectors.

title: A Training-Free Regeneration Paradigm: Contrastive Reflection Memory Guided Self-Verification and Self-Improvement
abstract: Verification-guided self-improvement has recently emerged as a promising approach to improving the accuracy of large language model (LLM) outputs. However, existing approaches face a trade-off between inference efficiency and accuracy: iterative verification-rectification is computationally expensive and prone to being trapped in faulty reasoning, while best-of-N selection requires extensive sampling without addressing internal model flaws. We propose a training-free regeneration paradigm that leverages an offline-curated contrastive Reflection Memory (RM) to provide corrective guidance, while regenerating from scratch helps break out of faulty reasoning. At inference time, the method performs RM-guided self-verification followed by a single RM-guided regeneration, avoiding both iterative correction and multi-sample selection. We evaluated our method on nine benchmarks that span algorithmic, reasoning, symbolic, and domain-specific tasks in both small- and large-scale LLMs. Experiment results show that our method outperforms prior methods while maintaining low computational cost.

evidence.title: A Training-Free Regeneration Paradigm: Contrastive Reflection Memory Guided Self-Verification and Self-Improvement
evidence.abstract: Verification-guided self-improvement has recently emerged as a promising approach to improving the accuracy of large language model (LLM) outputs. However, existing approaches face a trade-off between inference efficiency and accuracy: iterative verification-rectification is computationally expensive and prone to being trapped in faulty reasoning, while best-of-N selection requires extensive sampling without addressing internal model flaws. We propose a training-free regeneration paradigm that leverages an offline-curated contrastive Reflection Memory (RM) to provide corrective guidance, while regenerating from scratch helps break out of faulty reasoning. At inference time, the method performs RM-guided self-verification followed by a single RM-guided regeneration, avoiding both iterative correction and multi-sample selection. We evaluated our method on nine benchmarks that span algorithmic, reasoning, symbolic, and domain-specific tasks in both small- and large-scale LLMs. Experiment results show that our method outperforms prior methods while maintaining low computational cost.
evidence.venue: arXiv (Cornell University)

title: ALICE: A Multifaceted Evaluation Framework of Large Audio-Language Models' In-Context Learning Ability
abstract: While Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) have been shown to exhibit degraded instruction-following capabilities, their ability to infer task patterns from in-context examples under audio conditioning remains unstudied. To address this gap, we present ALICE, a three-stage framework that progressively reduces textual guidance to systematically evaluate LALMs' in-context learning ability under audio conditioning. Evaluating six LALMs across four audio understanding tasks under two output constraint categories, we uncover a consistent asymmetry across all stages and LALMs: in-context demonstrations reliably improve format compliance but fail to improve, and often degrade, the core task performance. This suggests that LALMs can glean surface-level formatting patterns from demonstrations but may struggle to leverage cross-modal semantic grounding to reliably infer task objectives from audio-conditioned examples, highlighting potential limitations in current cross-modal integration.

title: When Contextual Inference Fails: Cancelability in Interactive Instruction Following
abstract: We investigate the separation of literal interpretation from contextual inference in a collaborative block-building tasks, where an agent must resolve underspecified instructions using context. We adapt an existing two-speaker psycholinguistic paradigm into an interactive benchmark called Build What I Mean (BWIM). This setup contrasts a pragmatically cooperative speaker with one who is only literally reliable. In BWIM, models face underspecified instructions and must choose between making a contextual inference or requesting clarification at a small communication cost. Evaluating several state-of-the-art LLMs, we find a clear dissociation between judgment and action. Although models successfully detect speaker unreliability in explicit confidence ratings, they fail to leverage this awareness when taking action. Instead of deploying efficient clarification strategies, models default to suboptimal behaviors. These include partner-blind over-clarification and question-averse guessing under uncertainty. BWIM provides a controlled environment to evaluate online partner adaptation and contextual reasoning in interactive settings.

title: Gradient Magnitude Asymmetry as a Structural Honesty Mechanism in Multi-Agent World Model Communication
abstract: We investigate whether strategic deception emerges in multi-agent systems that coordinate through shared world model latent representations. Classical cheap talk theory predicts that diverging interests degrade message fidelity, yet we show this does not occur under standard dual-objective training. We propose gradient magnitude asymmetry (GMA) as the responsible mechanism: dense, per-timestep accuracy gradients systematically overpower sparse policy gradients from strategic reward. In 60 training runs across a 3×3 factorial design (reward divergence × verification) with ablations, totaling 467 GPU-hours, we find that (1) incentive divergence produces no significant change in belief-message divergence (p=0.86), (2) sweeping the accuracy weight β yields a monotonic increase in distortion (r=−0.97), and (3) partial verification independently reduces distortion by 38%. These results suggest that representation integrity in shared world models may be a designable property governed by the accuracy-to-strategic gradient ratio.

title: The Propagation Gap: Hidden-State Reliability Signals Do Not Reach Language Model Outputs
abstract: Language models report near-identical confidence on questions they reliably answer and questions they answer only intermittently. We introduce CI-Bench, a 338-question factual benchmark that assigns model-relative labels to each question: Known (K, ≥90% stochastic accuracy), Depth-ignorant (D, 20–80%), or Coverage-ignorant (C, <20%). The taxonomy distinguishes unreliable knowledge (D) from absent knowledge (C), a distinction that standard benchmarks conflate. Across six architectures, depth ignorance is model-relative: no question is classified D by all models, and D rates range from 0.9% to 28.1%. Behavioural screening shows that four of five models with sufficient D items report confidence within 3 percentage points of their K-item confidence, despite accuracy gaps exceeding 40 points. Hidden-state probes in three open-weight models decode a K-vs-D reliability signal at AUROC ≈ 0.76, concentrated in middle transformer layers. Surface-form controls confirm that this signal is absent from input features. Two structurally different single-pass output readouts (logit-distribution features and verbalized confidence) both plateau at AUROC ≈ 0.56–0.63, yielding a propagation gap of 0.18–0.19 AUROC (P < 0.001). The models encode reliability information that their output channels do not surface. CI-Bench, along with the labelling protocol and all code, is publicly released at github.com/raeq/propagation-gap.

title: Local Knowledge Mining of Architectural Heritage Semantic Fragments Based on Knowledge Graph Alignment
abstract: In the field of digital architectural heritage, the mining of tacit local knowledge embedded in architectural heritage is considered essential for the preservation, inheritance, and application of regional architectural characteristics. Local knowledge can be formally represented through semantic models, by which the automated mining of tacit information can be facilitated. However, due to the incomplete preservation of physical buildings and the fragmented nature of historical records, local knowledge is often represented as semantic fragments. Consequently, existing semantic models are still challenged in terms of knowledge integration and reasoning. In this study, a knowledge graph was developed for representing local knowledge, in which fragmented local semantics were aligned at both the ontological and entity levels. Subsequently, implicit local knowledge mining is achieved through meta-path centrality propagation combined with expert evaluation on a graph visualization platform. The method was applied to eight historical buildings in a case study. The knowledge graph quality assessment results indicate excellent ontology utilization and property utilization. The knowledge mining results demonstrate that graph-based expert evaluation successfully enables knowledge Feature Ranking and knowledge Extinction Warning.

title: "Synthetic Executable Companion to \u201cExploring Large Document Repositories with RDF Technology: The DOPE Project\u201d"
abstract: "This dataset and documentation package present a synthetic executable companion to the paper \u201cExploring Large Document Repositories with RDF Technology: The DOPE Project.\u201d Generated with the DBbun pipeline, the companion translates key ideas from the source paper into an inspectable computational artifact, including thesaurus-based indexing with EMTREE, RDF-based querying across heterogeneous repositories, co-occurring keyword analysis, hierarchy-aware query expansion, and visualization-oriented exploration of large biomedical document collections. The original paper describes a system that integrates major sources such as Medline and ScienceDirect through a semantic layer designed to support richer discovery and navigation.The generated companion includes a simulator, documented parameters, six simulation scenarios, structured CSV outputs, and multiple figures intended to make the paper\u2019s mechanisms more reusable for experimentation, teaching, and demonstration. According to the documentation, the package contains 22 parameters, of which 13 were extracted from the paper and 9 were assumed, and it covers scenarios such as aspirin-query retrieval, query-expansion depth sweeps, multi-keyword overlap complexity, and user-study-inspired feedback summaries.This resource is intended as a reproducibility-oriented, synthetic companion artifact rather than a reconstruction of the original authors\u2019 validated results. The simulator outputs, datasets, and figures are computationally inspired by the source document and are provided to illustrate the phenomena described in the paper, not to reproduce the original experimental data. Users should therefore treat this package as a supplementary executable interpretation of the paper."

title: Cooperative Task Allocation and Path Optimization of UAV Swarm Based on Genetic-Particle Swarm Hybrid Algorithm
abstract: To overcome traditional algorithms’ limitations (slow convergence, susceptibility to local optima), this study proposes a hybrid genetic-particle swarm algorithm (GPSHA). Integrating GA's global exploration with PSO's rapid convergence via adaptive parameters, GPSHA first establishes a multi-objective model incorporating flight range, time, obstacle avoidance, and task uniqueness constraints. Enhanced by PSO's position-speed update and adaptive crossover-mutation, the hybrid algorithm combines global and local optimization. Simulations show ≥15% faster convergence and 12% lower objective cost, effectively meeting drone swarm collaborative operation requirements.

title: Semantic Network Embedding with Gaussian Distributions
abstract: Knowledge graph embedding aims to represent human knowledge in a machine-interpretable form, enabling downstream language models to better incorporate structured information. Semantic network, as a special form of knowledge graph, organizes abstract conceptual knowledge in a hierarchical structure. Existing knowledge graph embedding methods struggle to preserve the inheritance property inherent in semantic networks. Therefore, in this paper, we propose a novel semantic network embedding framework, SN2E. We interpret abstract concepts as Gaussian distributions in a continuous space, using their mean vectors and covariance matrices as embeddings. Furthermore, we formally implement two fundamental semantic operators—intersection and subsumption. Based on this formulation, we develop an iterative algorithm to efficiently construct and train semantic network embeddings. We build two standardized semantic network datasets and conduct comparative experiments against several state-of-the-art knowledge graph embedding methods on classification tasks. The results demonstrate substantial improvements over existing approaches, and visualization analyses further confirm the rationality of our learned embeddings.

title: Drone Delivery Route Planning for the Low-Altitude Economy: An Improved Gray Wolf Optimization Algorithm Based on Niche Technology
abstract: With the rapid development of the low-altitude economy, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly used in logistics and e-commerce delivery services. Efficient route planning is a key factor affecting the safety, energy consumption, and operational efficiency of UAV delivery systems. However, traditional path planning algorithms often face challenges such as premature convergence and insufficient adaptability in complex low-altitude environments. To address these issues, this paper proposes an improved grey wolf optimization algorithm based on niche technology (NGWO) for UAV delivery route planning. The proposed method integrates a niche-sharing mechanism into the grey wolf optimization framework to enhance population diversity and avoid local optima. Meanwhile, a multi-objective route planning model is constructed by considering flight distance, energy consumption, obstacle avoidance, and delivery efficiency within the low-altitude logistics network. Simulation experiments conducted in a three-dimensional urban environment demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms and Genetic algorithms (GA) traditional GWO in terms of path optimality, convergence speed, and solution stability. The results indicate that the improved algorithm can effectively support UAV logistics operations and provide a reliable optimization framework for the development of the low-altitude economy.

title: Pattern-Aware Graph Neural Networks for Handling Missing Data
abstract: Missing data is ubiquitous in real-world datasets. Traditional methods either discard incomplete samples or apply imputation techniques that ignore potentially informative missingness patterns, implicitly assuming that missingness occurs randomly. However, missingness patterns might provide additional information. We propose pattern-aware graph neural networks that explicitly encode which features are missing alongside observed values. We used four encoding strategies-learned embeddings, frozen random embeddings, statistical features, and hierarchical representations-across seven UCI datasets with naturally occurring missingness. Our Pattern-aware methods achieve substantial improvements over baselines, with an average improvement of $17 \%$ in balanced accuracy and $22 \%$ in F1-macro across all datasets. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/TranMinett/pattern_aware_GRAPE.

title: Decoding AI authorship: can LLMs truly mimic human style across literature and politics?
abstract: Abstract Amidst the rising capabilities of generative AI to mimic specific human styles, this study investigates the ability of state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs), including GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro, and Claude Sonnet 3.5, to emulate the authorial signatures of prominent literary and political figures: Walt Whitman, William Wordsworth, Donald Trump, and Barack Obama. Utilizing a zero-shot prompting framework with strict thematic alignment, we generated synthetic corpora evaluated through a complementary framework combining transformer-based classification (BERT) and feature-based machine learning (XGBoost). Our methodology integrates Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) markers, perplexity, and readability indices to assess divergence between AI-generated and human-authored text. Results demonstrate that AI-generated mimicry remains highly detectable, with XGBoost models trained on a restricted set of eight stylometric features achieving accuracy comparable to high-dimensional neural classifiers. Post-hoc feature importance analysis indicates that perplexity is the most influential discriminative metric, suggesting systematic differences in the distributional regularity of AI outputs relative to the greater variability observed in human writing. While LLMs exhibit distributional convergence with human authors on low-dimensional heuristic features, such as syntactic complexity and readability, they do not yet fully replicate the nuanced affective density and stylistic variance inherent in the human-authored corpus. By isolating measurable statistical divergences in current generative mimicry, this study provides a structured benchmark for LLM stylistic behavior and offers insights for authorship attribution in digital humanities and social media contexts.

title: FAAR: Efficient Frequency-Aware Multi-Task Fine-Tuning via Automatic Rank Selection
abstract: Adapting models pre-trained on large-scale datasets is a proven way to reach strong performance quickly for down-stream tasks. However, the growth of state-of-the-art mod-els makes traditional full fine-tuning unsuitable and difficult, especially for multi-task learning (MTL) where cost scales with the number of tasks. As a result, recent studies investigate parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) using low-rank adaptation to significantly reduce the number of trainable parameters. However, these existing methods use a single, fixed rank, which may not be optimal for differ-ent tasks or positions in the MTL architecture. Moreover, these methods fail to learn spatial information that cap-tures inter-task relationships and helps to improve diverse task predictions. This paper introduces Frequency-Aware and Automatic Rank (FAAR) for efficient MTL fine-tuning. Our method introduces Performance-Driven Rank Shrink-ing (PDRS) to allocate the optimal rank per adapter location and per task. Moreover, by analyzing the image frequency spectrum, FAAR proposes a Task-Spectral Pyramidal Decoder (TS-PD) that injects input-specific context into spatial bias learning to better reflect cross-task relationships. Experiments performed on dense visual task benchmarks show the superiority of our method in terms of both accuracy and efficiency compared to other PEFT methods in MTL. FAAR reduces the number of parameters by up to 9 times compared to traditional MTL fine-tuning whilst improving overall performance. Our code is available.

title: The Semantic Binding Engine
abstract: The Semantic Binding Engine: Solving the Ontology Translation GapModern projects generate vast amounts of heterogeneous data—RFID pings, timesheet entries, BIM elements, sensor telemetry, drone imagery, and administrative records. Yet none of these systems share a common ontology. They describe the same real‑world event using incompatible languages, leaving critical relationships invisible and forcing humans to manually reconcile data that should already be unified.This gap is the Missing Ontology Translation Engine: the absence of a mechanism capable of understanding that multiple signals, across multiple systems, all refer to the same underlying task, activity, or physical state.The Semantic Binding Engine provides this missing layer.It is an AI‑driven semantic translator that automatically binds unstructured physical telemetry to structured administrative representations. Using spatial‑temporal proximity, behavioural patterns, and Large Language Models (LLMs), the engine identifies when disparate signals—such as an RFID location ping, a timesheet row, and a 3D BIM polygon—represent the same real‑world action. These signals are merged into a single Unified Node Identity, eliminating the need for manual data entry or cross‑system reconciliation.By resolving semantic fragmentation, the engine enables REM to maintain a coherent, continuously updated relational model of the project or asset. This ensures that design truth, administrative truth, and physical truth remain aligned, and that conflicts or anomalies can be detected and resolved at the relational level rather than through isolated system checks.The Semantic Binding Engine forms a foundational component of REM’s cognitive architecture, enabling automated interpretation, conflict detection, and system‑level coherence across complex, multi‑modal environments.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Its Role in Modern Industries: Applications, Challenges, and Future Trends
abstract: Artificial Intelligence and Its Role in Modern Industries: Applications, Challenges, and Future Trends Parth Aland Saint Thomas English Medium School, Solapur, India Dr. Rajivkumar Mente Dept. of Computer Applications, School of Computational Sciences, Punyashlok Ahilyadevi Holkar Solapur University, Solapur, India Dr. Preeti Deshmukh Dept. of Computer Science Engineering, V.V.P. Institute of Engineering & Technology, Solapur, India Dr. Bapu Chendge Dept. of Computer Applications, Central University of Karnataka, Kalburgi, India Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a transformative force in modern industries by enabling intelligent automation, data-driven decision-making, and adaptive operational systems. Advances in machine learning, deep learning, analytics, and Industry 4.0 have accelerated AI adoption across sectors. This paper reviews AI’s evolution, core techniques, applications, benefits, challenges, and future directions in industries such as manufacturing, healthcare, finance, logistics, energy, and retail. It examines how AI improves operational efficiency, reduces costs, enhances product quality, and supports workforce augmentation. At the same time, it highlights major challenges, including data quality, cybersecurity risks, ethical and legal concerns, lack of explain ability, high implementation costs, and workforce skill gaps. The study also discusses emerging trends such as explainable AI, autonomous industrial systems, Industry 5.0 integration, and sustainable green AI. By identifying research gaps and future opportunities, the paper supports responsible, scalable, and sustainable AI adoption for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Industry 4.0, Industrial Automation, Machine Learning, Smart Manufacturing, Industry 5.0

title: pkCNN:A scalable Zero-Knowledge proof for Convolutional Neural Network based on Plonk
abstract: Directly applying compute-intensive tasks in CNN models to general-purpose zero-knowledge proof systems is insufficient to meet practical requirements, as the computational complexity of proof generation and the scale of arithmetic circuits are directly correlated with the amount of computation. Therefore, improving the efficiency of circuit generation is a critical issue that urgently needs to be addressed. This paper proposes pkCNN, which splits the computations in CNN models into two parts for processing. It optimizes the verification of matrix multiplication, a common operation in linear computations, reducing its complexity to O(N). It also converts complex non-linear operations into constraints applicable to the Plonk system. Additionally, the Cached Quotients technique is introduced and enhanced with zero-knowledge properties, which is applied to the Lookup operations derived from the conversion of non-linear operations. The overall running time of pkCNN is approximately 1.5× faster than Baseline, while the SRS size is significantly reduced.

title: Seeing What Few-Shot Learners See: Contrastive Cross-Class Attribution for Explainability
abstract: Few-shot learning (FSL) enables deep learning models to generalize to unseen categories with minimal labeled data, making it crucial for data-constrained domains such as healthcare. However, existing FSL models often lack explainability, obscuring the reasoning behind their predictions and limiting trust in their deployment. In this work, we introduce contrastive cross-class attribution (C3A) to enhance explainability in FSL. Specifically, we present C3A for explaining query predictions and its variant (C3A-E) for episodic learning. Unlike prior explainability methods designed for specific architectures, our approach is classifier-agnostic, leveraging the backbone network to ensure broad applicability across diverse FSL paradigms. In addition, we propose contrastive local descriptors that integrate naive-Bayes nearest-neighbor (NBNN) and Fisher score-based attribution to preserve fine-grained details and enhance interclass discrimination. Finally, we comprehensively evaluate our methods across four FSL benchmarks, demonstrating consistent improvements over state-of-the-art approaches, with absolute gains of 19.72% in insertion-area-under-curve (iAUC) and 25.88% in deletion-area-above-curve (dAAC). Our posthoc design ensures seamless integration with various architectures, including Conv64F, ResNet12, ResNet18, and ViT. The experimental results confirm that C3A and its variant (C3A-E) provide more stable and interpretable explanations compared to existing FSL explainability methods, offering deeper insights into the episodic learning process. We have made our code publicly available at https://github.com/MountainChenCad/C3A.

title: A TD3 Approach Based on Two-Sided Evolutionary Fusion for Robotic Arm Path Planning
abstract: A Two Side Evolutionary Fusion-Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TEA-TD3) method is proposed focused on low planning efficiency along with long and tortuous paths for robotic arm path planning. Firstly, TEA-TD3 utilizes the Improved Cross-Entropy Method (ICEM) to alternately optimize the actor network and the critic network of TD3, thereby obtaining a better critic policy and improving the overall convergence speed. Secondly, hybrid distribution evolutionary perturbation mechanism and elite individual recycling mechanism are proposed. These mechanisms balance the scope of initialization perturbations for the actor network population and reintroduce the best critic network individual from the previous generation into the current population, thereby enhancing the overall explorative capability and stability of the method. Finally, the robotic arm conducts path planning experiments in the Robot Operating System (ROS)-Gazebo simulator. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms the ICEM-TD3 and TD3 methods in terms of success rate, average path length, average distance to the target, and average steps to completion.

title: Enhancing Cross-Document Entity Coreference Resolution with Argument Role Semantics
abstract: Cross-Document Entity Coreference Resolution (CDECR) aims to identify and link entity mentions across multiple documents that refer to the same real-world entity. Existing approaches typically rely on direct similarity computations between mentions or utilize local contextual information. However, these methods often struggle to maintain stable alignment when faced with cross-document stylistic variations and noise. While Large Language Models have recently provided new avenues for cross-document semantic understanding, their inherent hallucinations and the noise generated by divergent descriptions can lead to false positives or false negatives. To address these challenges, we propose a Cross-Document Entity Coreference Resolution method enhanced by Argument Role Semantics. We utilize a lightweight set of event argument role labels as robust semantic constraints to guide the LLM in generating accurate entity explanations integrated with full-document context. Through a direct joint representation learning technique, we inject entity explanations into the representation space to bolster the model's coreference resolution capabilities in cross-document scenarios. Our method's CoNLL F1 score surpasses the baseline by 0.9% on the ECB+ dataset, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach.

title: Bridging AI and Sustainability: The Role of Explainable AI in Climate Policy and Ethical Decision-Making
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as an integral part of modern-day environmental governance. It has been used as a supporter or facilitator in various domains like climate modeling, energy demand simulation, and monitoring of biodiversity. However, despite this progress, there have been various challenges arising from the lack of understanding of complex models of machine learning. The said challenge has become critical in the domain of sustainable scenarios because of their longer-term implications on nature and society. This has led to the advent of an important concept called Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), which has made it possible to understand these models and even point out factors influencing them and defining certain levels of uncertainties. The said literature has been predominantly technical and lacks pervasion into decisionsupport systems and governance of scenarios like climate change. This particular study has made an attempt to compile literature from 2023-2025 and presents a conceptual understanding of its applicability in decision-support systems of climates. To fill such gaps, this paper proposes the Policy Aligned Explainability Framework (PAEF), which aligns explanation techniques with requirements from the governance perspective, offering rolespecific explanation results, guidelines for evaluation, and compliance-friendly artifacts such as model cards, explanation reports, and monitoring logs. By proposing such a framework, the paper illustrates its application through two examples, which are demand response forecasting for the energy domain and early warning for forest deforestation through remote sensing. It also sees environmental sustainability and explainability through the perspective of governance.

title: Rapid optimization design of plate-type lifting lugs using an improved backpropagation neural network
abstract: Aiming at the common challenges in the traditional design of plate-type lifting lugs, such as structural redundancy and low iteration efficiency, this paper proposes a rapid lightweight optimization design method based on an improved backpropagation neural network. With the goal of structural lightweighting, a hybrid neural network model integrating particle swarm optimization and genetic algorithm is constructed. Leveraging its powerful nonlinear mapping capability, the model replaces traditional finite element trial calculations and achieves fast optimization of design parameters. A validation through seven practical engineering cases demonstrates that, under the premise of satisfying the same safety factors and working condition constraints, the proposed method significantly outperforms traditional design schemes, achieving a structural weight reduction of over 30% in all cases. Compared with that of the traditional particle swarm optimization algorithm, the optimization effectiveness of the proposed method is improved by approximately 14%. The results confirm the validity and reliability of this approach, providing a new technical pathway for the rapid optimization design of non-standard load-bearing components.

title: Development of an artificial intelligence-based computer-aided detection system for routine gastric biopsy diagnosis
abstract: To reflect real-world pathology practice, we developed an artificial intelligence-based pathological computer-aided detection system, trained on diverse epithelial and non-epithelial tumors for gastric biopsy specimens. A multicenter cohort comprising samples from six institutions was used for training and validated with an independent dataset from a seventh institution. We applied two distinct algorithms and three operational validity levels with optimized parameters to address the complexity of pathological diagnosis, reflecting routine diagnostic practice. Our system enabled the detection of malignant regions at low-magnification observation, aligning with the practical workflow of pathologists. In a reader study involving a limited number of test samples, the use of system assistance was associated with an improvement in diagnostic sensitivity. Further analysis revealed that samples with small and dispersed malignant foci had a higher rate of false-negative diagnoses, underscoring the potential of our system to improve diagnostic sensitivity. This study highlights the promise of integrating our system into real-world practice to aid pathologists in the routine diagnosis of gastric biopsy specimens.

title: An Agentic Approach to Generating XAI-Narratives
abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) research has experienced substantial growth in recent years. Existing XAI methods, however, have been criticized for being technical and expert-oriented, motivating the development of more interpretable and accessible explanations. In response, large language model (LLM)-generated XAI narratives have been proposed as a promising approach for translating post-hoc explanations into more accessible, natural-language explanations. In this work, we propose a multi-agent framework for XAI narrative generation and refinement. The framework comprises the Narrator, which generates and revises narratives based on feedback from multiple Critic Agents on faithfulness and coherence metrics, thereby enabling narrative improvement through iteration. We design five agentic systems (Basic Design, Critic Design, Critic-Rule Design, Coherent Design, and Coherent-Rule Design) and systematically evaluate their effectiveness across five LLMs on five tabular datasets. Results validate that the Basic Design, the Critic Design, and the Critic-Rule Design are effective in improving the faithfulness of narratives across all LLMs. Claude-4.5-Sonnet on Basic Design performs best, reducing the number of unfaithful narratives by 90% after three rounds of iteration. To address recurrent issues, we further introduce an ensemble strategy based on majority voting. This approach consistently enhances performance for four LLMs, except for DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp. These findings highlight the potential of agentic systems to produce faithful and coherent XAI narratives.

title: Discovery and Analysis Methodology of Hidden Instructions in Typical Embedded Processors
abstract: With the exponential growth in the complexity of the ARMv9-A architecture, the proliferation of its functional features has objectively widened the behavioral gap between the architectural specification and its microarchitectural implementation, making the verification of “hidden instructions” within the specification's undefined space a focal point in system security research. Existing studies are predominantly limited to the x86 architecture or early ARM versions evaluated via a single tool, lacking authentic data support on modern, complex microarchitectures. This paper proposes a probing methodology combining static double-blind cross-validation with physical-device dynamic Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation. Utilizing Capstone and LLVM to independently evaluate the entire AArch64 encoding space, billion-scale concurrent testing is conducted on a Radxa Orion-O6 development board equipped with the CIX P1 SoC (ARMv9.2-A Cortex-A720/A520). Experiments reveal that the consistently undecodable space accounts for up to 62.14%; in the bare-metal dynamic probing, all tested high-risk candidate instructions triggered an illegal instruction exception (SIGILL), and no valid hidden instructions were found. This result physically verifies the strictness of the target chip's decoding logic. Concurrently, it reveals a decoding conflict of up to 136 million instructions between heterogeneous analysis tools, providing a novel empirical reference for evaluating the reliability of underlying security tools.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Model Agents for Automated Scientific Literature Review Generation
abstract: This study investigates a method that integrates retrieval-augmented mechanisms into large language model agents for scientific literature review generation. The approach addresses the limitations of traditional review models that rely on parametric knowledge with insufficient timeliness and limited coverage. Incorporating external document retrieval and dynamic information fusion into the generation process enhances the accuracy and completeness of the output. The overall framework consists of query encoding, semantic retrieval, document filtering, knowledge fusion, language modeling, task planning, memory storage, and reinforcement optimization, forming a closed loop of retrieval, understanding, and generation. Relevant document fragments are first retrieved through semantic vector search to ensure comprehensive and reliable information sources. These external representations are then integrated with the internal embeddings of the language model through weighted fusion, which preserves fluency while maintaining factual grounding. The task planning module constrains logical flow and text structure, and reinforcement learning optimization further improves relevance and consistency. Comparative experiments on large-scale scientific literature datasets demonstrate that the method outperforms existing approaches on ROUGE, BLEU, METEOR, and diversity metrics, validating its effectiveness and practicality. The findings show that combining retrieval augmentation with agent architectures can significantly improve coverage, accuracy, and language quality in review generation, providing a feasible solution for knowledge organization in complex literature environments.

title: Research on the Prediction Method of Recent Photovoltaic Power Generation Based on CNN BiGRU
abstract: In response to the fluctuation and intermittency of output caused by large-scale grid connection of photovoltaic power plants, high-precision daily power prediction is crucial for ensuring system power balance and frequency stability. Therefore, this article proposes a CNN-BiGRU hybrid prediction model based on fuzzy C-means (FCM) clustering. This method first integrates historical photovoltaic power, numerical weather forecast (NWP) meteorological data, and four types of weather scene labels automatically divided by FCM to construct a multisource input feature set; Secondly, local spatiotemporal features are extracted through CNN and then input into BiGRU to mine bidirectional temporal dependencies, achieving end-to-end accurate modeling. Finally, experiments based on one-year measured data from a certain photovoltaic power station showed that the introduction of FCM clustering significantly outperformed benchmark models such as CNN and BiGRU in different seasonal scenarios in August and November. Among them, MSE decreased by 23.63%, MAPE decreased by 37.27%, and$R^{2}$increased by 0.012. The results verified the high accuracy and strong robustness of the proposed framework under complex meteorological conditions, which can provide effective decision support for power grid scheduling under high proportion photovoltaic grid connection.

Finally, experiments based on one-year measured data from a certain photovoltaic power station showed that the introduction of FCM clustering significantly outperformed benchmark models such as CNN and BiGRU in different seasonal scenarios in August and November. Among them, MSE decreased by 23.63%, MAPE decreased by 37.27%, and$R^{2}$increased by 0.012. The results verified the high accuracy and strong robustness of the proposed framework under complex meteorological conditions, which can provide effective decision support for power grid scheduling under high proportion photovoltaic grid connection.

title: UzSentiment Sentiment Analysis Methods for Uzbek Texts
abstract: This article is devoted to modern methods of sentiment analysis in Uzbek texts and the practical experience of applying them. The study compares two main approaches Naive Bayes and Support Vector Machine (SVM) - theoretically and practically, based on a corpus called UzSentiment, which consists of 100,000 texts labelled with positive and negative tags. The article begins with a literature review of existing international and Uzbek-language research in the field of sentiment analysis, highlighting the key challenges faced by lowresource and morphologically rich languages. Then, the selected models are described in detail with their mathematical formulations (Bayesian probability, margin optimisation). All models are trained on the UzSentiment corpus and evaluated using Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-score, with results compared through tables. The findings show that SVM achieves higher accuracy compared to Naive Bayes, while both approaches offer advantages in terms of computational efficiency. Additionally, the strengths and weaknesses of each method, optimisation opportunities for the Uzbek language, and practical application scenarios are examined. This study focuses on classical machine learning approaches, while deep learning models are considered beyond the scope of this work.

title: Hold the Prompt (HODPOT): Defense Design for Securing the System Prompt of LLM Agents
abstract: Since the public release of ChatGPT, generative AI (GenAI) models have become increasingly functional and autonomous, spurring their integration into a wide range of products. This integration introduces substantial security risks, most notably prompt-injection attacks that can manipulate model outputs and expose proprietary data. A less-studied variant—prompt-theft, where an adversary who fully controls the user prompt extracts the system prompt or a semantically equivalent paraphrase—remains viable even against state-of-the-art models. We formalise this threat under an attacker model that can issue arbitrary user inputs and observe the model’s responses. Our defense is a lightweight post-inference similarity filter: each generated output is compared using text similarity measures with a calibrated threshold that determines whether the response is returned unchanged, sanitized, or blocked. Experiments on eight LLMs and two “guard”-type models show that the filter reduces successful prompt extraction two-third of occurences while preserving above $90 \%$ of benign responses. These findings, given the the increasing usage of fully-autonomous GenAI agents, re-highlight prompt theft as a pressing research problem and motivate further work on adaptive thresholds, multi-modal prompts, and compositional leakage.

title: A sentiment-driven framework for early detection of emerging business trends through multi-platform social media analytics
abstract: Social media sites provide warning signs for shifts in consumer behavior, competitive forces, and emerging market trends. However, most small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs) do not have a systematic and scalable approach to tap into this unstructured data from various sites to extract insights. This paper proposes a trend detection method that leverages automated data extraction with n8n workflows, transformer-based embeddings, hybrid sentiment analysis, BERTopic clustering, and a weighted TrendScore composite score. The proposed approach combines multiple, heterogeneous inputs into a single analytical workflow and offers explainable visual and conversational BI interfaces, which are specifically designed for SMBs. The parameter definitions, scoring rules, and workflow diagrams are carefully detailed to ensure that the approach is fully reproducible. The proposed approach focuses on interpretability, robustness across multiple platforms, and applicability within a resource-constrained business setting. • Reproducible multi-platform social data acquisition using exportable n8n workflows. • Hybrid Transformer-Lexicon sentiment modeling combined with BERTopic clustering. • Quantified TrendScore integrating growth, engagement, sentiment shift, and cross-platform consistency.

title: Comparative Analysis of Linguistic and Stylistic Characteristics of Human and Artificially Generated Media Texts
abstract: The rapid rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has created a new linguistic challenge: distinguishing human from machine-produced media texts. Understanding the cognitive, stylistic, and pragmatic characteristics of AI-generated content is crucial for evaluating its impact on communication quality and reliability. This study aims to identify and characterize linguistic and stylistic features of AI-generated media texts compared to authentic journalistic publications. Corpus, stylometric, cognitive-pragmatic, and discursive analyses were employed to assess lexical, syntactic, semantic, and rhetorical dimensions. Results indicate that texts produced by models such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and BingAI exhibit higher grammatical accuracy, standardized syntax, reduced metaphoricity, and lower emotional expressiveness than human texts. Five parameters—grammatical variability, semantic richness, pragmatic relevance, rhetorical organization, and stylistic expression—determine the “humanness” of a text. A classification of stylistic models and linguistic markers was developed to identify text origin and evaluate its cognitive and communicative depth. The findings have practical applications for automated detection of AI authorship, enhancing digital media literacy, and establishing ethical standards for AI use in journalism and communication.

title: Opacity, Accountability, and Normativity: Toward a Right to Explanation or Justification?
abstract: While technical advancements in transparency are essential, they alone cannot fully resolve the challenges posed by AI opacity. To establish a robust framework for accountability in the digital era, it is imperative to ensure that AI systems operate not only transparently but also justifiably, aligning their decisions with broader moral, political, and legal principles. The chapter begins in section 5.1 by reconstructing when this debate started in the AI field and what is the XAI movement. Section 5.2 investigate how the distinction between justification, motivation and explanation within the philosophy of action, can clarify—or complicate—this debate. Section 5.3 delves into Kate Vredenburgh’s conceptualization of the Right to Explanation arguing that, unlike narrower definitions that focus solely on technical transparency, her framework incorporates a crucial normative dimension. Section 5.4 examines Rainer Forst’s theory of the Right to Justification, comparing it to Vredenburgh’s proposal and demonstrating how Forst’s approach also provides a comprehensive normative framework for accountability that can be useful to tackle the problem of opacity and other broader worries connected with AI. Finally, Section 5.5 examines what achieving true accountability would entail in practice, emphasizing the necessity of mechanisms that ensure meaningful and robust justifications.

title: Design and Implementation of a Deep Learning-Based Big Data Analysis System for Tumor Diagnosis
abstract: This paper proposes a deep learning-based big data system for tumor-assisted diagnosis. The framework integrates two-stage transfer learning, a lightweight DenseNet-MobileNet hybrid network with channel attention, and a Spark-based distributed architecture. The system improves feature extraction under limited data and enhances computational efficiency. Experiments show an F1 score of 97.12%, outperforming baseline models by 4.3% while achieving 21.3% faster inference.

title: Enhanced Part-of-Speech Tagging Resources and Models for Tigrinya
abstract: Part-of-speech (POS) tagging is one of the fundamental tasks in natural language processing, with many downstream applications. For low-resource languages like Tigrinya, the development of robust POS taggers remains challenging due to complex linguistic features and limited annotated datasets. This work presents a newly constructed larger Tigrinya POS Corpus (TiPOSC24), comprising over 118 K tokens annotated with 12 distinct POS classes, significantly expanding the resources available for Tigrinya NLP research. We leverage state-of-theart transformer models, particularly TiRoBERTa, achieving a weighted $\mathbf{F 1}$-score of 95.6%, an improvement of 5.6 percentage points over the previous best result. We present through error analysis to idenitify remaining challenges. Our findings demonstrate the effectiveness of pretrained language models for morphologically rich languages and contribute to bridging the resource gap for Tigrinya language processing.

title: EWA-DA: An EWA-Learning-Based Double Auction Mechanism for Multi-Agent Task Allocation
abstract: Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) are increasingly deployed in complex scenarios like the Internet of Things and cloud computing, where efficient task allocation remains challenging. Centralized allocation methods face computational bottlenecks and vulnerability to single-point failures. This paper models multi-agent task allocation as a double auction game, with agents acting as buyers or sellers of task resources. We present the Experience-Weighted Attraction based Double Auction (EWA-DA) algorithm, which combines reinforcement learning with belief learning. Agents adjust their bidding strategies using both their historical rewards and predictions of other agents' behaviors. Our simulation experiments show that EWA-DA converges rapidly to Nash Equilibrium and achieves higher system utility than baseline methods across different conditions. The proposed mechanism offers a decentralized approach to resource allocation in MAS.

title: Regression Prediction of Communication Signal Bit Error Rate under Anti-interference Based on Machine Learning Algorithms
abstract: During the operation of modern communication systems, the complexity of the electromagnetic environment is constantly increasing, and the existence of various artificial and natural interferences seriously affects the stability of signal transmission, posing a great challenge to the precise prediction of communication signal signal-to-noise ratio and bit error rate. Machine learning algorithms, with their core advantages of being able to extract potential correlations from massive measured data and not relying on precise mathematical modeling, provide a new solution path for this problem. However, existing machine learning algorithms still have shortcomings such as insufficient feature extraction and slow model convergence speed in communication signal prediction applications. To address these issues, this paper proposes the DE-Transformer-BiLSTM regression algorithm. Firstly, it processes the data through correlation analysis and violin plot analysis, and then conducts comparative experiments by combining multiple machine learning algorithms. The experimental results show that the prediction performance of this algorithm is significantly superior to other traditional machine learning algorithms. Its mean square error, root mean square error, and mean absolute error are the lowest among all models, the average absolute percentage error remains at a low level, the coefficient of determination is as high as 0.988, and the fitting degree and prediction accuracy are both optimal. This research provides effective technical support for improving the signal transmission stability and prediction accuracy of modern communication systems.
